exercises.title: Nói: long turn theo khung 4 phần
exercises.instruction: Chỉ 30 giây chuẩn bị (ghi từ khoá), rồi ghi âm nói liên tục ít nhất 75 giây theo đủ 4 phần. AI chấm theo 4 tiêu chí.

items.prompt: Describe a friend you have known for a long time. You should say: who this person is · how you met · what you usually do together. And explain why this friendship matters to you.
items.sampleAnswer:
**[INTRODUCTION] **I'd like to talk about my best friend Minh, who I've known for almost fifteen years — since our very first week of primary school.

**[DESCRIPTION] **First of all, he's an easy-going, funny person, and we still live only about ten minutes apart. What I remember most is the day we met. I'd forgotten my lunch, and this small boy I'd never spoken to just broke his bánh mì in half and handed it to me without saying a word. These days we usually meet for coffee every Saturday morning, or play badminton when we both have time.

**[WHY IT IS SPECIAL] **The reason I chose Minh is that he's one of the very few people I can be completely honest with. When I failed my driving test last year, he didn't try to cheer me up with jokes — he just booked another test date for me and made me practise with him every evening.

**[CONCLUSION] **Overall, Minh is more like a brother than a friend, and I honestly can't imagine my life without him.
items.sampleNote: Đủ khung 4 phần của Lesson 1 với ít nhất 3 chi tiết cụ thể (tên, mười lăm năm, ổ bánh mì ngày đầu gặp, lần thi trượt bằng lái). Kết bằng một câu tổng kết — không "That's all".

The reason I chose this is that… → Overall,…

exercises.title: Nói: từ 6 từ khoá thành 90 giây
exercises.instruction: 30 giây ghi chú CHỈ từ khoá (tối đa 8), rồi ghi âm nói 90 giây phát triển từ đúng trang ghi chú đó. Liếc giấy tối đa 3 lần.

items.prompt: Describe a building you often see or visit. You should say: where it is · what it looks like · how it is used. And explain how you feel about it.
items.sampleAnswer:
I'd like to talk about the old Central Post Office in Ho Chi Minh City, which is just a ten-minute ride from my university. It's a grand yellow building from the French colonial period, with tall arched windows and a huge clock right above the entrance.

The moment you walk in, what strikes you first is the light — it pours in through the glass roof and makes the whole hall feel bright and calm, even at midday. There's also a faint smell of old paper from the counters where people still send letters and parcels.

I usually go there two or three times a month, sometimes to post things for my mother, but more often just to sit on the wooden benches and read for half an hour. It's surprisingly quiet considering how many tourists pass through.

For me it's more than just a building — it's a reminder that some parts of the city have barely changed in a hundred years, and I find that oddly comforting.
items.sampleNote: Từ khoá gốc: bưu điện TP / 10 phút · vàng, cửa vòm, đồng hồ · ánh sáng, mùi giấy · 2–3 lần/tháng · đọc sách · "not just a building". Mỗi từ khoá được mở rộng 3–5 lớp, có hai chi tiết cảm giác (ánh sáng, mùi giấy cũ).

items.prompt: Describe a place you often go to in your free time.
items.sampleAnswer:
I'd like to talk about a small café on Nguyen Hue Street, which is only about a five-minute walk from my house. It's quite a modest place — dark wooden furniture, maybe eight tables, and they play old jazz records rather than the usual pop music. The moment you walk in, the smell of roasted coffee hits you, and somehow the noise of the street just disappears.

I usually go there on Sunday mornings and stay for about three hours studying. Honestly, I get more done in those three hours than in a whole day at home. There are no distractions, no family members asking me to do things, and the wifi is deliberately slow — which I think is a genius business decision.

What makes it special, though, is the owner. She's an elderly woman who has run the place for over twenty years, and after a few months she started remembering my order and even my name. That small thing gives you a real sense of belonging.

Overall, it's become a sort of second living room for me, and I honestly can't imagine my weekends without it.

items.prompt: Describe a photograph you like. You should say: what is in the photo · when and where it was taken · who took it. And explain why you like it.
items.sampleAnswer: The photograph I'd like to describe is one that has been on my desk for years, which is a picture of my grandmother in her garden. It was taken about ten years ago, on a bright winter morning, and my uncle took it without her noticing — she's half-laughing at something off-camera. **[2] BACKGROUND ▸ **At the time, I was in my second year, and four of us were working on a project about social media. It all started when our lecturer asked each group to give a ten-minute presentation. One of my groupmates, Thu, was very shy, and she'd been worrying about her part for days.

**[4] RESOLUTION ▸ **In the end, our group got one of the highest marks in the class.

**[5] REFLECTION ▸ **Looking back, it taught me that helping someone doesn't always mean doing the work for them — sometimes it just means giving them a way to start. Afterwards I felt genuinely proud, and a little relieved myself.

**INTRODUCTION ▸ **The habit I'd like to develop is reading for twenty minutes every morning instead of checking my phone. It's something I got into about six months ago, after realising I hadn't finished a single book in a year.

**WHAT IT IS ▸ **My routine is quite simple: I leave my phone in the kitchen overnight, make a coffee as soon as I get up, and then read on the balcony until my breakfast alarm goes off.

**YOUR PROGRESS ▸ **At first, I could barely manage five minutes — my hand kept reaching for my phone out of habit. Over time, I gradually built it up by keeping the book on my pillow so it was the first thing I saw, and by choosing short, easy novels rather than heavy textbooks. Nowadays I manage it about four mornings a week, which is a big improvement, but I'd love to make it every single day.

**WHY YOU WANT IT ▸ **The main reason is that it's genuinely stress-relieving — I start the day feeling calm rather than rushed. It also helps me build discipline, which carries over into my studies.

**CONCLUSION ▸ **So overall, it's a small habit, but I think it could make a real difference in the long run.

I still remember how hard it was at the beginning — I could barely switch between two chords, and my fingertips would hurt after just a few minutes. items.prompt: CUE CARD — Describe a person who has had an important influence on your life. You should say: who this person is · how you know them · what they have done. And explain why they have influenced you.
items.sampleAnswer:
I'd like to talk about my old English teacher, Mrs Hoa, who taught me for three years in high school — and we've kept in touch ever since.

What stood out about her was her patience. She had this habit of never showing surprise, no matter how basic your question was. I remember failing a test in Year 11 and expecting a lecture — instead, she sat with me after class for almost an hour and worked through every question as if we had all the time in the world. She also showed me how to keep a vocabulary notebook, which I still use today.

The reason she influenced me so much is that she changed how I deal with things I find difficult. Before her class I used to give up quickly and decide I just wasn't good at languages. She made me believe that struggling with something didn't mean I couldn't do it.

Overall, Mrs Hoa left a lasting impression not because her English was perfect, but because she was unshakeably patient — and I still try to be that way when I'm explaining something to someone else.

items.prompt: Follow-up 1 — Do you think people are influenced more by family or by friends?
items.sampleAnswer: It changes with age, I think. When you're young, family shapes almost everything — your values, your habits, how you see the world. But as you move into your teens and twenties, friends and the wider environment start to matter more, because that's where you test those values against other people's. So I'd say family sets the foundation and friends do the fine-tuning.

items.prompt: Follow-up 2 — Is it important to have role models when you are young?
items.sampleAnswer: Yes, genuinely important. A good role model gives you a concrete picture of what's possible, and it's much easier to aim for something you've actually seen someone do. That said, they don't have to be famous — often the most useful role models are ordinary people close to you, like a teacher or an older relative, precisely because their life feels within reach.

items.prompt: CUE CARD — Describe an occasion when something did not go as planned. You should say: when it happened · what you had planned · what actually happened. And explain how you dealt with the situation.
items.sampleAnswer:
I'd like to tell you about a trip that went wrong when I tried to visit a friend in another city.

It happened about a year ago. The plan was simple: take an early coach, spend the day with her, and come back the same evening. I'd booked the tickets a week in advance and even screenshotted the route.

The key moment came about an hour into the journey, when the coach broke down on the motorway. We sat on the hard shoulder for nearly two hours waiting for a replacement, and by the time it arrived my phone battery had died, so I couldn't even tell my friend what was happening.

In the end, I got there four hours late, we only had about ninety minutes together, and I had to leave almost immediately to catch the last coach back.

Looking back, though, those ninety minutes were oddly memorable — we laughed about the whole disaster the entire time. It taught me that a plan falling apart isn't always a bad thing; sometimes it's the part of the trip you actually remember.

items.prompt: Follow-up 1 — Do you think it is better to plan everything or to be flexible?
items.sampleAnswer: A loose plan works best for me — enough structure to feel prepared, but enough flexibility to adapt when things change. Planning every detail just means more things can go wrong, and you spend the whole time stressed about the schedule instead of enjoying it. So on balance, I'd say plan the important parts and leave the rest open.

items.prompt: Follow-up 2 — How do people in your country usually react when plans change?
items.sampleAnswer: Fairly calmly, in my experience. There's a general acceptance that traffic, weather or last-minute changes are just part of life, so people tend to shrug and improvise rather than get upset. Older generations are especially relaxed about it; younger people, who grew up with everything scheduled through apps, can find it a bit more frustrating.

Câu 1 — CUE CARD — Describe an occasion when something did not go as planned. You should say: when it happened · what you had planned · what actually happened. And explain how you dealt with the situation.
I'd like to tell you about a trip that went wrong when I tried to visit a friend in another city.

It happened about a year ago. The plan was simple: take an early coach, spend the day with her, and come back the same evening. I'd booked the tickets a week in advance and even screenshotted the route.

The key moment came about an hour into the journey, when the coach broke down on the motorway. We sat on the hard shoulder for nearly two hours waiting for a replacement, and by the time it arrived my phone battery had died, so I couldn't even tell my friend what was happening.

In the end, I got there four hours late, we only had about ninety minutes together, and I had to leave almost immediately to catch the last coach back.

Looking back, though, those ninety minutes were oddly memorable — we laughed about the whole disaster the entire time. It taught me that a plan falling apart isn't always a bad thing; sometimes it's the part of the trip you actually remember.

Câu 2 — Follow-up 1 — Do you think it is better to plan everything or to be flexible?
A loose plan works best for me — enough structure to feel prepared, but enough flexibility to adapt when things change. Planning every detail just means more things can go wrong, and you spend the whole time stressed about the schedule instead of enjoying it. So on balance, I'd say plan the important parts and leave the rest open.

Câu 3 — Follow-up 2 — How do people in your country usually react when plans change?
Fairly calmly, in my experience. There's a general acceptance that traffic, weather or last-minute changes are just part of life, so people tend to shrug and improvise rather than get upset. Older generations are especially relaxed about it; younger people, who grew up with everything scheduled through apps, can find it a bit more frustrating.

items.prompt: CUE CARD — Describe a place you would recommend to a visitor to your country. You should say: where it is · what people can do there · who you would recommend it to. And explain why you would recommend it.
items.sampleAnswer:
I'd like to talk about Da Nang, a coastal city in central Vietnam, roughly halfway between Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City.

The first time I visited was about three years ago, and the moment I stepped onto My Khe Beach and felt the sea breeze, I was completely won over — the water was clear, the sand was almost empty early in the morning, and the whole place felt refreshing after months of city life.

What really stands out is the variety. You can spend the morning on a pristine beach and be up in a mountain resort thirty minutes later. The food is excellent too, especially the seafood, and it's noticeably cheaper than in the bigger cities.

I'd recommend it to almost anyone, but especially to first-time visitors who want a bit of everything without the crowds of Hanoi or Saigon. The pace is more relaxed and the people are very easy-going.

Overall, it's the place I always suggest first, and I've been back twice myself since that first visit — there's always something new to try.

items.prompt: Follow-up 1 — Has tourism changed your country in recent years?
items.sampleAnswer: Quite significantly. Tourism has brought real economic benefits — jobs, investment, better infrastructure in a lot of coastal towns. But those benefits are unevenly spread: in the most popular spots, long-term residents are being priced out and the character of the place changes as shops start catering only to visitors. So it's been positive overall, but not without costs.

items.prompt: Follow-up 2 — Do you think tourists should learn about local culture before travelling?
items.sampleAnswer: I think a bit of effort goes a long way — learning a few phrases and understanding basic customs, for example around temples or removing your shoes. It shows respect and it genuinely improves the experience. I'd stop short of expecting people to study a place in depth, but arriving with zero awareness often leads to misunderstandings that could easily be avoided.
